Plan a Marswalk the way the rovers scouted it.

A layered planner for two of the best-mapped places on Mars — Jezero Crater, where Perseverance landed in an ancient lake, and Gale Crater, where Curiosity is climbing Mount Sharp into the boxwork formations. Every fact, image and route stop here comes from the NASA and USGS sources linked on this page. The planner’s map is the real thing: genuine NASA Mars Trek tile layers, streamed live from trek.nasa.gov — the same Viking, MOLA, THEMIS and HiRISE mosaics Mars Trek itself stacks.

Two landing sites, two different science stories

The challenge brief suggests starting where a rover has already done the scouting. Both sites below qualify — pick one in the planner and the map, waypoints and science goals change with it.

Mars 2020 · Perseverance

Jezero Crater — the ancient lake

Jezero is a ~45 km impact crater at the northwestern edge of the Isidis basin, in the Nili Fossae region (18.4°N, 77.7°E). It once held a lake: two inlet valleys, Neretva Vallis and Sava Vallis, cut the western rim and built a river delta, and an outlet valley, Pliva Vallis, breaches the eastern rim. The crater floor lies at about −2,600 m elevation.

Perseverance touched down on 18 February 2021 at the Octavia E. Butler Landing, near the junction of the Máaz and Séítah formations and about 2 km from the western delta front. In its first science campaign (sols 100–379) it traversed more than 5 km and studied both formations.

Marswalk science goal: walk the crater-floor formations to the delta front — reading lake sediments and igneous floor rocks in one traverse.

Mars Science Laboratory · Curiosity

Gale Crater — the mountain of layers

Gale is 154 km (96 mi) across at 5.4°S, 137.8°E. At its centre, Aeolis Mons — Mount Sharp — rises about 5 km (NASA describes it as ~3 miles, ~5 km; the mound stands 5.5 km above the northern floor) from the crater floor: a stacked record of Martian climate history.

Curiosity landed on 6 August 2012 at Bradbury Landing (4.5895°S, 137.4417°E) in Aeolis Palus, inside a 20 × 7 km landing ellipse, and has been climbing lower Mount Sharp since 2014. Since May 2025 it has been investigating the boxwork unit — the brief’s example science target.

Marswalk science goal: climb from the clay-bearing unit through the sulfate-bearing unit to the boxwork and Gediz Vallis — walking upward through Mars’s drying climate.

The layered map — built on NASA Mars Trek

This is a real Mars Trek map, not a picture of one. The tiles stream live from NASA’s Solar System Treks WMTS service (trek.nasa.gov) — the exact service the Mars Trek portal itself uses. Pick a basemap, stack overlays on top of it and drag their opacity sliders to blend layers the way Trek does, switch between Jezero and Gale, zoom from the whole planet down to the 25 cm/px HiRISE mosaic of the landing sites, and tap any numbered waypoint for its field notes. Drag to pan, scroll or pinch to zoom; the readout under the map tracks your cursor’s Mars coordinates. Want the map by itself? Open it on its own full page → — and use the 2D Map / 3D Planet switch above the map to spin Mars as a globe.

What each layer actually is — and where it comes from

No layer on this page is decorative — the planner above serves these exact products as Mars Trek WMTS tile layers. Mars Trek is the tool that stacks them natively: per NASA’s description, it layers high-resolution Mars data products in 2D and Globe view and provides elevation profiles, sun-angle calculations, Sun and Earth position, 3D-printing output, and bookmarks for exploration areas by mission.

Optical

Orbital + rover cameras

HiRISE and CTX images from Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter form the detailed base maps (the Curiosity planned-route mosaic, for example, is a HiRISE mosaic). At ground level, Perseverance’s raw image gallery holds over 1 million images from the rover’s journey — the astronaut’s-eye preview of every stop.

Open the Perseverance raw images gallery ↗

Topographic

MOLA elevation & DEMs

The topographic maps in the USGS Mars map set are based on the Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter (MOLA) on Mars Global Surveyor — more than 600 million measurements gathered 1999–2001. Mars Trek turns the same elevation data into profiles, so a planner can see the climb before walking it.

Open Mars Trek ↗

Geologic

USGS global geologic map

The USGS-led global geologic map of Mars (Tanaka and others, 2014; USGS SIM 3292) brings together observations from four orbiting spacecraft over more than 16 years. Its headline finding: the Martian surface is generally older than previously thought — three times as much of it dates to the Early Noachian Epoch as was previously mapped.

USGS: New Global Geologic Map of Mars ↗

Thermal

THEMIS infrared base

Detailed geologic mapping is tied to a photogrammetrically controlled 100-metre-per-pixel base derived from THEMIS (Thermal Emission Imaging System) daytime infrared data. Thermal behaviour helps distinguish loose sediment from hard rock underfoot — a mobility question, not just a science one.

Example: USGS Athabasca Valles geologic map ↗

Spectral / mineralogy

Clays, sulfates, carbonates

Orbital spectra are why these routes exist: orbiters detected strong clay signals in Mount Sharp’s clay-bearing unit and sulfates above it, and Jezero was mapped with crater floor, delta and marginal carbonate units before landing. On the ground, Perseverance’s SuperCam collected 1,450+ chemistry observations and a similar number of VISIR spectra in its first 286 sols alone.

JPL: Curiosity planned route (HiRISE mosaic) ↗

Traverse

Where the rovers actually went

A Marswalk route is only credible if a wheeled vehicle already survived the terrain. Perseverance covered more than 5 km in its crater-floor campaign; Curiosity had driven 17.63 km and gained 327 m of elevation by sol 1856 at Vera Rubin Ridge — and is still climbing. The traverses in the planner follow these documented routes and named stops.

JPL: Curiosity’s route to Gediz Vallis channel ↗

The two traverses, stop by stop

Read them as EVA itineraries: each stop is a real, named rover location with the science the mission actually did there. Distances and elevations are the missions’ published figures, not estimates added for this page.

Traverse A · Jezero

Crater floor → delta front

StopWhat’s there
Octavia E. Butler LandingTouchdown site, 18 Feb 2021, ~2 km from the delta front. Traverse elevations here start around −2,570 m.
Máaz formationBasaltic crater-floor unit; dominant lithology along the early traverse is basaltic, with plagioclase.
Séítah formationOlivine-rich unit explored on the southward traverse — rover elevations reached −2,583 m at Rochette (sol 168) and −2,584 m on sol 171; Artuby ridge rises to about −2,580 m.
Western delta frontWhere Neretva Vallis water entered the lake and dropped its sediment — the mission’s prime ancient-lake target.
Pliva Vallis (context)The outlet valley on Jezero’s eastern side, ~50 km long — evidence the lake once filled and drained. A regional landmark, not a one-EVA walk.

Campaign total: >5 km traversed, 7 abrasion patches, sols 100–379 (crater-floor campaign).

Traverse B · Gale

Bradbury Landing → boxwork

StopWhat’s there
Bradbury LandingTouchdown site, 6 Aug 2012, Aeolis Palus. Named for author Ray Bradbury on 22 Aug 2012.
Yellowknife BayIn 2013 the mission found evidence here of an ancient freshwater-lake environment offering the basic chemical ingredients for microbial life.
Vera Rubin RidgeBy sol 1856 (25 Oct 2017): +327 m elevation gained, 17.63 km driven from landing.
Clay-bearing unitStrong clay signals from orbit — clays point to past water. A priority target since before Curiosity launched.
Sulfate-bearing unitSulfate minerals may indicate the area was drying up or becoming more acidic in ancient times.
Gediz VallisA channel ~300 ft (91 m) wide cut through the sulfate unit — possibly carved by an ancient river or debris flows. Its centre holds mounds of boulders and a debris ridge from landslides and water-induced flows from above.
Boxwork unitAltadena member, Mirador formation: erosion-resistant ridges ~5 m across intersect into polygons ~10–20 m across and 1–2 m deep — interpreted as fractures cemented by diagenetic fluids. Curiosity began investigating it on sol 4534 (8 May 2025).

Route visual: NASA’s annotated flyover labels these same regions on the proposed route up lower Mount Sharp.

Safety first: planning the walk, not just the science

NASA’s first priority is astronaut safety, and the challenge brief names the constraints directly: a radiation environment unlike Earth’s, spacesuit-limited mobility while carrying science equipment, and obstacles such as large rock formations. The planner below keeps those constraints in view — it does not invent weather or radiation numbers; for current conditions you go to the linked NASA tools.

Visor HUD · preview

What the walker sees

The HUD mirrors the planner’s selected waypoint: name, why it matters, and the hazard the rover record warns about. Switch waypoints in the planner above and this readout follows.

Work in pairs, plan the retreat

The brief asks crews to consider working in pairs and using rovers or robotic systems to carry tools and supplies. Both traverses here follow ground a rover has already crossed, so the retreat path is proven terrain — and every waypoint lists the obstacle (boulder fields in Gediz Vallis, 1–2 m-deep boxwork hollows, loose Séítah troughs) that a suited walker must plan around.

What you’ll actually see on the walk

Point-of-view imagery from the surface missions, so the crew knows the terrain before they’re standing in it. For the full, searchable set — over a million Perseverance images — use the raw images gallery.

The five resources — use the real tools

Everything above is a planning layer over these sources, not a replacement for them. These are the exact resources from the challenge brief.

JPL Mars Trek ↗

NASA’s web-based portal for exploration of Mars. It showcases data collected by NASA at various landing sites, with layering and viewing of high-resolution data products in 2D and Globe view, plus elevation profiles, sun-angle calculations, and mission bookmarks. marstrek.jpl.nasa.gov

USGS–NASA Planetary Geologic Mapping Program ↗

The high-quality, standardized geologic map of Mars: the USGS-led global geologic map (Tanaka and others, 2014) built from four orbiters’ data, with the topographic companion set based on MOLA’s 600M+ laser-altimeter measurements.

Curiosity route map visual — Mount Sharp ↗

The brief’s example: an animation showing a proposed route for Curiosity climbing lower Mount Sharp, with an annotated map labelling the regions scientists want to explore — clay unit, sulfate-bearing unit, Gediz Vallis — and a flyover explaining them. See also JPL’s HiRISE planned-route mosaic ↗.

NASA Worldview ↗

Visually explore the past and present of a dynamic planet from a satellite’s perspective — part of NASA Earthdata. Included in the brief as the model for layered, time-aware satellite exploration; apply the same layer-and-compare workflow to Mars in Mars Trek. worldview.earthdata.nasa.gov

Mars Perseverance Raw Images Gallery ↗

Over 1 million images captured by the rover on its journey across the Martian surface — the ground-truth, point-of-view layer for every Jezero waypoint. mars.nasa.gov/mars2020/multimedia/raw-images/
